body.text: Israeli settler organisation founder Daniella Weiss sanctioned by Australian government
In short:
Daniella Weiss has been sanctioned by the Australian government.
She is among three individuals targeted by the government for illegal settlement expansion and human rights abuses against Palestinians in the West Bank.
What's next?
Travel bans against the individuals will be enforced, any assets they may have will be frozen and it is now illegal to work with these individuals and the entities they represent.
The woman widely regarded as the godmother of the Israeli settler movement has been hit with sanctions by the Australian government, along with the settlement advocacy group she founded and leads.
Daniella Weiss and her Nachala organisation are the latest to be subjected to Australian sanctions, announced this morning by the Foreign Minister Penny Wong.

She is among three individuals targeted by the Albanese government, and Nachala is one of four entities Senator Wong says are "involved in illegal settlement expansion and human rights abuses against Palestinians in the West Bank".

"The sanctioned individuals and organisations have actively participated in the planning, coordination and establishment of new settlements, including raising funds, recruitment of volunteers and providing support to violent settlers," the minister said in a statement.
The measures include making it illegal to work with the individuals and entities, with hefty fines for anyone and potential jail terms for those who do.
Any assets they may have will also be frozen, and travel bans against the individuals enforced.
"We are taking these actions because the rapid expansion of settlements and settler violence are extinguishing the possibility of a two-state solution,"
Senator Wong said.
"This includes the E1 settlement where demolitions and the displacement of Palestinians have occurred in recent weeks."
The E1 development, east of Jerusalem, has faced fierce opposition for many years.
It will effectively divide the West Bank in two and is seen as part of efforts to scuttle any hope for Palestinian statehood, which Australia joined other countries in recognising in late 2025.
The latest sanctions follow measures against two ministers in the Netanyahu government in July last year — far-right national security minister Itamar Ben-Gvir and Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich.
The two men, who themselves are settlers, were targeted due to their policies and rhetoric against the Palestinian population.

Australia and other countries have raised concerns about the surge in violence by settlers against the Palestinian community in recent years, which has hit record levels according to organisations such as the United Nations.
The Netanyahu government has been accused of allowing the violence to spread, and minimising its severity by claiming it is being perpetrated by a handful of young men from broken homes.
Israel is yet to respond to the Australian sanctions announcement.

It has previously torn up the visas of Australian diplomatic representatives to the Palestinian Authority in protest over the Albanese government recognising Palestinian statehood and blocking Israeli politicians entering the country on character grounds.
'A turning point'
Last year, the British government sanctioned Mrs Weiss. The European Union followed earlier this year.

When the ABC last interviewed Mrs Weiss, she was again advocating the Israeli settlement of Gaza and the expulsion of Palestinians in the war-ravaged strip, insisting the population needed to be "dispersed".
"They go to Africa, they go to Scotland, they go to England, they go to Europe, they go all over the world, not here," she said.
"This time, this period is over."
When asked whether she considered that ethnic cleansing, she responded that she called it "a turning point in history".
Nachala, the organisation she leads, uses a logo that reflects a biblical idea of "greater Israel".
It shows a map of the Middle East under Israeli control which stretches from Egypt's Sinai peninsula, across modern-day Israel, Palestine, Lebanon, Syria, Jordan and parts of Iraq and Saudi Arabia.

While Nachala's view of territorial expansion goes far beyond the policies espoused by the Netanyahu government, members of the right-wing coalition have backed Mrs Weiss's demands for settlement expansion in the occupied West Bank and Gaza.
Israeli settlements in the Palestinian territories are considered illegal under international law, and more than 750,000 settlers currently live in occupied East Jerusalem and the West Bank.
The Israeli government insists it has a right to settle in the West Bank, which it refers to by the biblical names of Judea and Samaria.
UK government sanctions settlers, builders
The Australian sanctions also target people involved in building settlements in the occupied West Bank, including Eilav Libi and Itamar Yehuda Levi, who run building and demolition companies.
Mr Levi's company, Eyal Hari Yehuda Company, is also now on the sanctions list. So too are two settlement expansion organisations, the Amana Settlement Association and Hashomer Yosh.
On Tuesday, the UK government announced its own sanctions against settlers and construction companies.
Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Sa'ar labelled the move "a hostile act targeting private, law-abiding companies".
"The Jewish people have the right to live in their historic homeland.
"As in the past, Israel will respond to the British government's actions with countermeasures."
The announcement from UK foreign secretary Ed Miliband came more than two months after he foreshadowed the move and flagged a ban on trade with settlements.
Most staff have left and it has lost its status as a consulate, but a small diplomatic presence remains to provide services to the Palestinian community.
In September, Senator Wong said Australia was considering its own measures but would not join the British-led efforts at that moment.
Soon after, the ABC revealed Australia had pulled out of joining at the 11th hour.

Western diplomatic sources in Israel had pointed to last month's election, and the possibility of a change in government, as a moment for a change in approach in how countries deal with Israel and the issues around settlements.
